3.text: marked difference between the two branches of the people. In many camps

4.text: in various parts of the territory of the Chukchee I have met very old men,

5.text: perhaps of seventy or even eighty years; at least, their hair was altogether

6.text: white, which change seems to occur among the Chukchee later than among

7.text: the white race. Some of these old men were almost in their dotage; still

8.text: they had retained possession of the herd and the general direction of life in

9.text: their camps. For instance, in a camp on the Oloi River, a man named

10.text: Kauˊno, who had great-grand-nephews ten years old, owned two large herds,

11.text: and decided himself the most important question in the seasonal migration of

12.text: the Chukchee, that of choosing the place of abode for the summer-time.

13.text: Though enfeebled by age, he still made the April trip to the Wolverene River

14.text: every spring for barter with the maritime traders from the Arctic villages,

15.text: who come there at that time, bringing maritime products and American wares.

16.text: Kauˊno’s own housemates told me that the old man had grown childish and

17.text: often purchased things of little use in their life. Instead of sugar he took

18.text: bottled molasses, because it was red, and red pleased his eye; he bought

19.text: table-knives instead of hunting-knives, because they are brighter, etc. This

20.text: was told, however, with broad grins, and without any visible signs of protest.

21.text: “Foolish one!” (Yurg̣umteˊq) they added quite good-humoredly. “What is to

22.text: be done? He is an old man!” (Qailoˊqɪm, miˊñkri, ɪnpɪnaˊčhɪn). And I am

23.text: quite sure that Kauˊno kept the direction of his house till his natural end.

24.text: Another old man of sixty on the Dry Anui had a dislocation of the hip-joint,

25.text: which was altogether out of service in walking. He could only crawl about

26.text: with the aid of two crutches. Therefore his name was Atkaˊ-Pañaˊnto (“Lame

27.text: Pañaˊnto”). His lameness dated from a bad fall in a wrestling-match in

28.text: which he took part. He was then married and the owner of a herd. He

29.text: continued to be the master of his herd and the head of his family, and had

30.text: several children, who grew up and took care of the herd. Every year he

31.text: would go to the Anui fair for barter, carrying along peltries and reindeer-

32.text: skins. He was very fond of strong liquor, bought it every time, and drank

33.text: most of it himself, giving to each of the other members of his family only a

35.text: At fairs and gatherings for trade, whenever I visited a camp for the first

36.text: time, those who came to meet me would say, “Let us take you to the oldest

37.text: man. Talk first to him.” Baron von Maydell mentions that when he travelled

38.text: in the country near the Upper Anadyr, a very old man from a remote camp,

39.text: who came to meet him, was carried for a long distance on the shoulders of

40.text: his young relatives.¹ This happened in summer, when sledges cannot be used.
